title: Video Review of Yourself
hook: The one body you can study with full consent and endless replays is the one you have never actually watched: your own.
why:
A manager is told in his annual review that he comes across as impatient in meetings. He is baffled. He likes his team, he listens carefully, and he feels interested, not impatient. He decides the feedback says more about the person who gave it than about him, and nothing changes. Two years later he hears the same word from someone else and still cannot see it, because he has never once watched himself listening.

Every other chapter in this book is about reading bodies you can only observe from outside, briefly, with partial knowledge and no right to replay. Your own body is the exception. You can record it, watch it slowly, compare it with what you felt at the time, and ask what a stranger would conclude. No other practice gives you a baseline you can check so precisely, or shows you so clearly how far your inner experience and your outer signal can drift apart. It is also, at first, deeply uncomfortable, which is why most people never do it.

teach.h: Everyone around you knows your body better than you do.
teach.p:
Think about how you usually see yourself: in a mirror, face on, still, usually adjusting something. You almost never see yourself in profile, from above, from across a room, while talking or listening, or in the unguarded moments between sentences. The people you live and work with see those views all day. You have been the least informed observer of your own body for your whole life.

Even the mirror misleads. It shows your face reversed, and in 1977 Theodore Mita, Marshall Dermer and Jeffrey Knight found that people tend to prefer the mirror image of their own face, while their friends prefer the true image, the one the camera shows. Each side prefers the version it is used to. This is why photographs of yourself can look subtly wrong: you are seeing the face everyone else knows and you do not.

The same is true of movement. Habits that are invisible from inside, a frown when concentrating, a hand that drifts to the jaw, a way of looking at the floor before answering, are perfectly visible from outside, and the people around you have been reading them, and sometimes misreading them, for years.

Video closes some of that gap. It gives you the outside view, the one you otherwise only hear about secondhand in reviews, arguments and offhand remarks, and it lets you check those remarks against evidence instead of against your intentions.

Use video rather than photographs. A still image freezes one unrepresentative instant, the half-blink, the mid-word grimace, and invites exactly the kind of single-frame reading this book warns against. Movement over minutes shows your range, which is what other people actually experience when they spend time with you.
teach.disconfirm: If your first few reviews show nothing you did not already know about how you move, you may be unusually aware of your own body. Ask someone who knows you well whether the video matches what they see before deciding that.

teach.h: The first viewing is for getting used to yourself.
teach.p:
Almost everyone hates the first recording. In the 1960s Philip Holzman and Clyde Rousey studied what they called voice confrontation: people hearing recordings of their own voices reacted with surprise and often distaste, while rating other people's recorded voices quite neutrally. Part of the reason is physical. You normally hear your own voice partly through the bones of your skull, which makes it sound lower and fuller to you than it does to anyone else. The recording is the voice everyone else hears.

Video adds the face, the posture and the gestures, and the discomfort multiplies. You will notice your weight, your hairline, the way your mouth moves, a dozen things that have nothing to do with reading people. That reaction is normal and it fades with exposure, usually within three or four viewings.

So treat the first viewing as an exposure session and nothing more. Watch the whole recording once, all the way through, without stopping, without notes and without deciding to change anything. Let the cringing happen. The goal is simply to reach the point where you can watch yourself as a body moving in a room, rather than as a list of flaws.

Do not make any decisions after the first viewing. Judgments made in the first flush of self-consciousness are about how you look, not about how you communicate, and they tend to produce exactly the wrong changes: stiffness, self-monitoring, a smile held too long.
teach.disconfirm: If you find yourself still unable to watch after four or five recordings, the discomfort is not fading by exposure alone. Try shorter clips, sound off, or watching with someone you trust, before deciding the practice is not for you.
teach.pullQuote: The first viewing is for getting used to yourself, not for deciding what to change.

teach.h: You show far less than you feel.
teach.p:
In 1998 Thomas Gilovich, Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Husted Medvec described the illusion of transparency: people consistently overestimate how much of their inner state others can see. Participants asked to lie, or to hide disgust while tasting something unpleasant, believed observers would see straight through them. Observers mostly did not.

Video review is one of the most direct ways to experience this. Researchers working on social anxiety, including Allison Harvey, David Clark and colleagues, found that people who believed they looked visibly anxious often looked far calmer on video than they expected, and that watching the recording after first predicting what they would see, and then watching as if it were a stranger, helped correct the belief.

For most men this is a relief and a lesson at once. The pounding heart before a presentation, the flush of embarrassment, the irritation in a meeting: much of it never reaches the surface, or reaches it far more faintly than it feels. You are less transparent than you fear.

The lesson runs the other way too. If your own strong feelings barely show, other people's may not show either. The friend who looks fine may not be fine. The colleague who seems calm may be churning. Video of yourself teaches you, in your own body, why a calm surface is weak evidence of a calm interior, which is one of the most important cautions in the whole book.

There are exceptions, and you should look for yours. Some signals show more than people expect: blushing, a tremor in the voice, rapid blinking, a flushed neck. Some people are simply more expressive than average. The recording will tell you which kind you are, and whether any particular signal of yours is unusually visible. That is far better than guessing in either direction.
teach.disconfirm: If your recordings consistently show your inner state as clearly as you feel it, you are an exception to a well-replicated effect, and you should expect other people to read you easily. Test it by asking someone who watched the same moment.

teach.h: Review in three passes: sound off, sound on, then as a stranger.
teach.p:
Once the first viewing has blunted the discomfort, review every recording in three passes.

*Sound off.* Watch only the body. Count self-touches and note when they cluster. Watch how often you gesture and with which hand, where your eyes go when you think, when your posture shifts. Without words to follow, you will see movement you would otherwise miss, just as you do with strangers in earlier drills.

*Sound on.* Now watch how the body lines up with the words. Where do the gestures fall: on the important word, or before it, or not at all? What happens to your face while the other person talks? When do you start moving before you start speaking, a sign you are waiting rather than listening?

*As a stranger.* Finally, watch once as if you had never met this person. Write three neutral sentences describing him, the kind a careful observer might write in a journal: *Leans back while listening, frowns slightly, glances at the laptop every few seconds; leans in and gestures broadly when speaking.* Then write what a stranger might reasonably guess from that, and whether the guess would be right.

The third pass is the one that changes people. It turns your own body into an object of the same disciplined observation you practise on others, and it shows you which of your habits are likely to be misread.

Choose your material deliberately. Five to ten minutes is enough; longer recordings rarely get the three passes they need. Record ordinary moments as well as hard ones, because the ordinary ones are your baseline and the hard ones only make sense against it. A recording every week or two, reviewed properly, teaches more than a daily one skimmed.
teach.disconfirm: If your stranger's description and your own sense of yourself match closely, the recording has confirmed you rather than surprised you. That is useful too, but record a more demanding situation before concluding there is nothing to learn.

teach.h: Compare what you felt with what was seen.
teach.p:
The most valuable thing video gives you is not a picture of your body but a measure of the gap between how you felt and how you looked.

Here is how to measure it. Record something with a little pressure in it: explaining a hard idea, answering difficult questions you set yourself, describing a painful memory. Immediately afterwards, before watching, write a short timeline of how you felt minute by minute, rating tension from one to ten. Then watch the recording and rate, minute by minute, how tense you look. Put the two lines side by side.

Most people find two kinds of gap. The first is the one the previous section described: moments of high inner tension that barely show. The second is less comfortable: moments when you felt relaxed or interested but looked something else entirely. Many men discover that their neutral face, especially when concentrating, reads as stern, annoyed or bored. They were thinking hard. They looked displeased.

The second kind of gap is where misreadings of you come from. Your colleagues are not wrong to read a hard frown as displeasure; they are reading what they can see. Knowing your own gaps lets you explain them, change them, or at least stop being baffled when people react to a face you did not know you were making.

Consider showing the two lines to one person you trust, someone who sees you often and will tell you the truth. Ask whether the seen line matches what they experience day to day. Their answer either confirms the recording or tells you it caught an unusual moment, and either is worth knowing. The next chapter is about building exactly that kind of honest mirror.
teach.disconfirm: If your felt and seen lines track each other closely across several recordings, your face is unusually expressive of your state, and people around you probably read you well. That is worth knowing in both directions.

teach.h: Change one habit at a time, and only the ones that cost you.
teach.p:
A careful review will show you a dozen habits. Most of them should be left alone. Fidgeting with a pen, a particular way of standing, a gesture you use too often: these are part of how you move, and people who know you read them correctly.

Choose only habits that cost you something with other people, usually because they are reliably misread. The concentrating frown that reads as disapproval. Looking at the floor before every answer in a culture where that reads as evasion. Starting to move toward the door several minutes before you leave. Pick one, never more.

Then design a small replacement rather than a suppression. Daniel Wegner's research on thought suppression found that trying not to think of something can make it come back more strongly, and trying not to do a habitual movement often produces stiffness or a different leak. A replacement works better: instead of not frowning, nod and say *go on*; instead of not looking at the floor, look at your notes.

Rehearse the replacement a few times, use it for two weeks, then record yourself in a similar situation and compare. If the new habit has replaced the old one without making you rigid, keep it. If you look stiff or self-conscious in the new recording, let it go; an awkward new habit is worse than a misread old one.

Be wary of changes made to look more confident, more dominant or more likeable. Those are performances, and people sense performances. The only changes worth making are the ones that let others read you more accurately: closing the gap between what you mean and what they see, not opening a new one.
teach.disconfirm: If the new recording shows the old habit unchanged, or replaced by a stiffer one, the replacement was not a good fit. Choose a different one rather than trying harder at the same suppression.

teach.h: Record only yourself, and never anyone without their consent.
teach.p:
Everything in this chapter is about recording your own body. It never extends to recording other people without their knowledge. Covert recording is illegal in many places and a breach of trust everywhere, and recordings of other people's faces and bodies are exactly the material this book refuses to build files from.

The safest practice is to record yourself alone: rehearsing a talk, explaining something to the camera, answering questions you have set. If you want to review how you come across in real meetings or calls, record only your own video feed, tell the people involved that you are doing it for your own practice, and follow any rules your workplace has. Many video platforms show a recording indicator to everyone, and that is as it should be.

Treat your own recordings as private. Store them on your device rather than an automatic cloud folder if you can, and delete them once you have reviewed them and written your notes. A file of you unguarded and uncomfortable is not something you want to turn up later, and the notes are what you need.

Finally, watch for the point at which review stops helping. A man who records every conversation to check how he came across has swapped one blind spot for another: constant self-monitoring, which makes people stiff, self-absorbed and less present. A recording every week or two is plenty.
teach.disconfirm: If you notice you want to record a conversation with someone in order to check how *they* behaved, the practice has drifted from self-review into surveillance. Do not record it.

caseStudy:
Alex, thirty-four, runs a team of six designers. In his annual review his director tells him that two people have said he comes across as impatient in meetings. Alex is stung. He thinks of himself as a careful listener, and he decides the comment is about one difficult designer who resents his decisions.

His partner suggests he look rather than argue. Alex tells the team he is going to record his own camera feed in their next two stand-ups, for his own practice, and deletes the files once he has made notes.

The first viewing is miserable: his voice sounds thin and he looks tired. He makes no notes. On the second pass, with the sound off, he sees something he has never noticed. Whenever anyone else speaks, his brow draws down hard, his eyes go to his laptop every few seconds, and his pen taps against the desk. When he speaks himself, he leans in, smiles and gestures broadly. On the third pass he writes the stranger's description: *Animated when talking; when listening, frowns, looks away, taps; seems keen for others to finish.*

His felt timeline from the same meeting says *interested, thinking about the design problem* for almost every minute he was frowning. He was not impatient. He looked it, reliably, for anyone who was not inside his head.

Alex chooses one habit. Instead of looking at his laptop while others speak, he closes it and nods when someone makes a point he wants to come back to. He leaves the frown alone, because it feels too deep to change. Two weeks later he records another stand-up. The frown is still there, but the glances away are gone, and the nods give people something to read.

At his six-month check-in his director mentions, without being asked, that the team says he seems more engaged in meetings. Alex says nothing about the recordings. He keeps the last set of notes in his journal, under a heading he has started using for his own baseline.
observe: On your next video call, glance at your own preview at three random moments and note your face and posture each time, then return your attention to the conversation.
Ask one person who sees you often what your face looks like when you are concentrating, and write down their answer without arguing with it.
The next time you feel sure your nerves are showing, note the moment, and afterwards ask someone who was there whether they noticed anything.

drills.name: The Three Passes
steps: Prop up your phone and record five minutes of yourself explaining something you know well, as if to a friend.
Watch it once all the way through with no notes, simply to get used to it.
Watch it again with the sound off and note self-touches, gestures and where your eyes go.
Watch it a third time as a stranger and write three neutral sentences describing the man on screen.
Write what a stranger might reasonably guess about his state, and whether that guess would be right.
variations: Do the three passes with a recording of yourself listening rather than speaking, since that is when many people's faces are most misread.
Ask a trusted friend to do the third pass on your recording, writing their own three neutral sentences, and compare them with yours.
Repeat the drill a month later on a similar task, and compare the two sets of notes.

drills.name: Felt Versus Seen
steps: Record ten minutes of yourself doing something with a little pressure in it, such as answering hard questions you wrote in advance.
Immediately afterwards, before watching, rate how tense you felt in each minute from one to ten.
Watch the recording and rate how tense you look in each minute.
Put the two sets of numbers side by side.
Mark the biggest gap in each direction and write one sentence about each.
variations: Try the drill with a low-pressure task as well, and compare the gaps with those from the pressured one.
Rate how warm or interested you felt, not just how tense, and compare those with what was seen.
Ask a friend to rate your recording minute by minute without seeing your felt ratings, and compare all three columns.

drills.name: Resting Face
steps: Record three minutes of yourself reading something dull in silence.
Watch it with the sound off and describe your face as a stranger would, in three plain sentences.
Write the most likely mood a stranger would guess from it.
Write the mood you were actually in.
Note one situation in your life where that gap could cause a misreading.
variations: Record your resting face at different times of day, morning and evening, and notice whether it changes.
Ask someone who sees you often what your resting face looks like to them, and compare their answer with yours.
Record yourself listening to someone on a call, and notice whether your listening face differs from your reading face.

drills.name: One Habit
steps: From your review notes, choose one habit that is likely to be misread by the people you work or live with.
Write a small replacement for it, something to do rather than something to stop.
Rehearse the replacement five times in front of the camera.
Use it in real conversations for two weeks.
Record a similar situation and compare it with the original.
variations: Choose a habit that is misread at home rather than at work, such as how you look when you are thinking, and work on that one.
Ask someone you trust to tell you, without your asking each time, when they see the old habit return during the two weeks.
Write down, after two weeks, whether the replacement now feels natural or still feels like a performance.

drills.name: Mirror and Camera
steps: Look at yourself in a mirror for one minute and note what you see.
Take a photo with the front camera, then view it unflipped so it matches what others see.
List the differences that stand out.
Note which version feels more like you, and which one everyone else knows.
Write one sentence about what that gap means for how you judge your own expressions.
variations: Try the drill with a photograph taken by someone else rather than a selfie, and notice which version your friends recognise.
Look at a video of yourself and notice whether your gestures seem to go the wrong way round, as mirror habits can make them feel.
Notice, for a week, how often you check your appearance in mirrors and screens, and what you look at first.

quiz.q: Why does a recording of your own voice usually sound wrong to you?
options: Recording equipment distorts voices, especially cheap phone microphones, making them thinner
You normally hear your voice partly through the bones of your skull, which makes it sound lower and fuller
Everyone's voice changes when they are being recorded, because they speak more carefully
Your memory of your own voice fades over time, so any recording sounds unfamiliar at first
quiz.explain: The recording is closer to what everyone else hears. Your own perception adds bone-conducted sound that no one else receives. The surprise is normal, and it fades as you get used to the outside version.

quiz.q: What did Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec's work on the illusion of transparency find?
options: That people can hide almost nothing from observers who are trained
That lying is nearly always visible on video when it is slowed down
That people underestimate how much of their emotion shows to others
People overestimate how much of their inner state others can see
quiz.explain: Participants believed their concealed feelings were obvious, and observers mostly could not see them. Video review lets you experience this directly. It is also a warning that other people's calm surfaces are weak evidence of calm.

quiz.q: In a review you see that you frown hard and look down whenever you are concentrating, and colleagues have called you stern. What should you do?
options: Treat it as one habit worth working on: practise a small replacement, such as a nod, and record again
Practise smiling more or less constantly in meetings, so that nobody can read you as stern
Ignore it, since you know you are not stern and your colleagues will come to see that
Tell your colleagues they are misreading you, and explain what the frown actually means
quiz.explain: The frown is costing you, because it is reliably misread. A small replacement is more likely to stick than suppression, and a second recording tells you whether it worked. A held smile is a performance, and people notice.

quiz.q: Why is the first review pass done with the sound off?
options: It is less embarrassing than hearing your own voice played back at you
Recordings on most phones are clearer to watch without the sound on
Without words to follow, you see movement you would otherwise miss
Sound tends to distract you from what your face is doing on the screen
quiz.explain: Words pull attention to meaning. With them gone, the body's rhythms, self-touches and gestures become visible, just as they do when you watch strangers with the sound off.

quiz.q: After a careful review you find twelve things you dislike about how you come across. What is the best approach?
options: Fix them all before your next meeting, while the recording is still fresh in your mind
Choose the one habit most likely to be misread by others and change only that, with a replacement
Delete the recording, and stop reviewing yourself, since the exercise is only making it worse
Practise a completely new posture and manner until it feels natural, and record again then
quiz.explain: Most habits should be left alone, because the people who know you read them correctly. Changing everything produces stiffness and self-monitoring. One habit that costs you, replaced rather than suppressed, is enough.

quiz.q: You want to review how you come across in your team's weekly meeting. What is the right way to record it?
options: Record the whole meeting without telling anyone, so that everyone behaves naturally in front of the camera
Record the whole meeting openly, and review how everyone else in it behaved as well as yourself
Record only your own feed, tell the team it is for your own practice, and delete it after making notes
Ask a colleague to film you from across the room, without telling the others what it is for
quiz.explain: Self-review is about your body, with consent from anyone else involved. Secret recording is unlawful in many places and a breach of trust everywhere. Deleting the file afterwards keeps the notes and loses the risk.

quiz.q: What did Mita, Dermer and Knight find in their 1977 study of photographs?
options: That people preferred their true image, while their friends preferred the mirror image of them
That people preferred their mirror image, while their friends preferred their true image
That neither people nor their friends could tell the true image from the mirror image
That everyone preferred whichever photograph had been taken in the better light
quiz.explain: People tended to prefer the mirror version of their own face, the one they see most, while their friends preferred the true image, the one they see most. That is part of why your photographs look subtly wrong to you.

quiz.q: A lecturer's students say he seems nervous. His recording shows constant pacing and jingling keys, though he felt calm throughout. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ignore the feedback, since he felt calm and that is what really matters
Change the habits that are being misread, one at a time, and record again
Stop moving altogether, holding himself completely still for every lecture
Fix every habit he can see on the recording in time for the next lecture
quiz.explain: The gap between what he felt and what was seen is exactly what review is for. Changing the one or two habits that are reliably misread, and checking with a new recording, closes it without making him stiff.

quiz.q: Someone says that recording an ordinary, uneventful day is a waste, and you should only review your big moments. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That ordinary days give the bad day a baseline, so it is worth recording them too
That ordinary days show nothing useful at all, since nothing goes wrong on them
That only recordings of other people's big moments are worth reviewing carefully afterwards
That big moments should never be recorded, since they make people too nervous
quiz.explain: A single recording of a bad day has no baseline, so you cannot tell which habits are always there and which appeared under pressure. Ordinary days show what your body does when nothing is wrong.

reflection.prompt: Describe one specific piece of feedback about how you come across that you have heard more than once, from different people, such as you seem distracted, you look annoyed or you seem nervous. Write down when you heard it and from whom, by role. Then describe one specific moment when the feedback might have been true from the outside, even if it was not true from the inside, and what someone watching you at that moment would actually have seen.
reflection.guidance: The aim is to set your intentions aside for a moment and imagine the camera's view. You know what you meant; the question here is what was visible. If you cannot think of a piece of feedback you have heard twice, write about the one you have heard once and dismissed most quickly, since quick dismissal is often a sign that it touched something. If you have already recorded yourself for this chapter, use what you saw. Keep the tone plain. This is not an exercise in self-criticism, only in noticing a gap that other people have been seeing for a long time.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to stop after the first viewing. The reader records himself, cringes at his voice and his face, deletes the file and decides video review is not for him. He never reaches the second and third passes, where the useful information is. The opposite failure is just as damaging: a man who becomes absorbed in his recordings, tries to fix every habit at once, and turns stiff and self-conscious in exactly the conversations he wanted to improve. Changing your body to look more confident or more likeable is not the goal. The goal is to see the gap between what you feel and what others see, and to close it only where it causes people to misread you. A third failure is ethical: using the practice as cover for recording other people. Record yourself, with consent from anyone else involved, and delete the files once the notes are written.

moreCases.title: The candidate with the bored face
moreCases.scene:
Funmi, twenty-seven, has been applying for marketing jobs for four months and has reached the final interview three times without an offer.
  The feedback each time is vague: "great answers", "not quite the right energy", "we weren't sure how engaged you were". She cannot understand it. She
  prepares carefully and cares a great deal about the jobs.

  A friend suggests she record a mock interview. Funmi props her phone on a pile of books, asks the friend to read out ten questions, and answers them
  as she would in a real interview. The first viewing is miserable. She hates her voice and makes no notes.

  On the second pass, with the sound off, she sees it. When she is answering, her face is lively: she smiles, her eyebrows move, her hands gesture. When
  her friend is asking the question, and for the first few seconds of every answer while she thinks, her face falls completely still. Her mouth turns
  down slightly at the corners, her eyes go to the side and her eyelids drop. With the sound off, it looks like boredom. On the third pass she writes
  the stranger's description: "Animated when speaking; when listening, looks bored, possibly irritated."

  Her felt timeline for the same minutes says "concentrating hard" every time.

She also notices that her habit of looking down while she thinks lasts three or four seconds, which in an interview feels like a long time from the other side of the table.

She also notices that, on the sound-on pass, her answers are good: clear, specific and warm. The problem was never what she said.
moreCases.misread:
The interviewers read Funmi's still, downturned face while she listened and thought as boredom or a lack of engagement. Funmi read her own rejections as a mystery, because she knew how much she cared, and could not see what they saw.

And her friends, who knew her well, had never mentioned her listening face, because they had long since learned to read past it.

The interviewers, too, had read her face for only a few minutes, with no baseline, which is exactly the setting in which a resting face is most easily misread.
moreCases.betterRead:
Gilovich, Savitsky and Medvec found that people overestimate how much of their inner state others can see, and video review exposes the reverse gap too: feelings that do not show at all. Funmi's concentration was real and invisible; her resting face, as the Resting Face drill demonstrates for many people, carried a mood she did not feel. This chapter's advice is to change only the habits that are reliably misread, and this one was. Her better approach was the One Habit drill: a small replacement for the listening face, rather than a performance. She practised a slight nod and a softening of the mouth as each question began, and a brief "That's a good question" before thinking, so that the pause read as thought. She rehearsed it five times on camera. At her next final interview, the feedback said "really engaged". She got the job.

She also kept the list of the things she simply disliked about her recording, as the chapter suggests, and then threw it away.

moreCases.title: The lecturer who did not know he paced
moreCases.scene:
Felix, forty-five, lectures in chemistry at a university, and he thinks of himself as a calm, steady presenter. In this year's student feedback,
  several comments mention his "nervous energy" and say that he is "hard to follow". One student writes that watching him is like watching a tennis
  match. Felix is puzzled and a little hurt. He does not feel nervous when he lectures; he has been doing it for fifteen years.

  The university's teaching centre offers to record one of his lectures, from the back of the hall, with the students' agreement and with only Felix
  in shot. He watches it in his office.

  On the second pass, with the sound off, he sees himself walk from one side of the stage to the other and back, over and over, at a steady pace,
  through the whole fifty minutes. His left hand jingles the keys in his pocket. When he reaches the board, he turns his back on the room and talks to it.
  He counts forty-three crossings of the stage.

  On the third pass, as a stranger, he writes: "Moves constantly; seems restless or anxious; talks to the board." His felt timeline from the lecture says
  "calm, enjoying it" for almost every minute.

He also notices that he talks faster when he walks, and slower when he stands still, which may be why the students found him hard to follow.

His colleague, a younger lecturer, tells him afterwards that she had noticed the pacing in his first lecture to her own class years ago, and had assumed he knew.
moreCases.misread:
The students read Felix's constant pacing and jingling keys as nervousness and found the lecture hard to follow. Felix had read his own calm as visible, and had no idea that his body was saying something quite different.

Felix also read the student comments as unfair, because he could not imagine how anyone could see nervousness in a man who felt none.

And the students read his back turned to the board as a lecturer who had forgotten them, when he was simply writing.
moreCases.betterRead:
The Felt Versus Seen drill measures exactly this gap: how you felt, minute by minute, against how you looked. Usually, as Gilovich and colleagues found, people show less than they feel. Felix showed more: a habit of movement that read as anxiety, though he felt none. Part IV's chapter on stage presence recommends moving on transitions and standing still for key points, and pacing throughout is the opposite. His better approach was to change one habit at a time. He took his keys out of his pocket before lectures, which removed the jingle at once. Then he practised the One Habit drill for the pacing: walk on transitions, plant his feet for each key result, and turn back to the room before talking about anything on the board. The next recording showed nine crossings. The following year's feedback called him "clear and easy to follow".

He also asked the teaching centre whether they could offer the same recording to new lecturers, which they now do.

moreCases.title: The salesman who fixed everything
moreCases.scene:
Wes, thirty-five, sells software to schools, and his manager has suggested that he review recordings of his video demos to improve. Wes takes
  it seriously. He records five demos and reviews each one carefully. By the end of the week, he has a list of fifteen habits he dislikes: touching his
  face, saying "basically", leaning too close to the camera, smiling too much, smiling too little, blinking a lot, looking at his notes, a slight lisp on
  certain words, and seven more.

  He decides to fix them all at once. In his next demo, he holds his face still, sits rigidly at a measured distance from the camera, keeps his hands out
  of shot, rations his smiles, avoids every word on his banned list and reads a script so that he does not have to look at notes.

  The demo is a disaster. A head teacher on the call asks, politely, whether he is feeling all right. Another says afterwards that it felt like talking to
  a recording. Wes's conversion rate for the month falls by half.

  His manager, Gemma, watches the recording with him. She says that she has never seen him look less like himself, and asks which three of the fifteen
  habits had actually cost him anything with a customer.

He has also started recording himself on every call, including calls with existing customers, and spending two hours each evening reviewing them.

He also notices, watching the stiff demo back, that he looks frightened, which is the opposite of what he had been trying to fix.
moreCases.misread:
Wes read every habit he disliked on the recording as a flaw to be removed, and his clients read the result, a stiff, scripted, rationed version of him, as someone unwell or not quite real.

His manager had read the original recordings as showing a good salesman with one or two small habits, which was much nearer the truth.

Wes also read Gemma's original suggestion as a sign that she thought he was doing badly, which is partly why he threw himself at the list so hard.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter's failure mode warns that a man who becomes absorbed in his recordings and tries to fix every habit at once turns stiff and self-conscious in exactly the conversations he wanted to improve. Changing your body to look more confident or likeable is not the goal; the goal is to close the gap between what you feel and what others see only where it causes people to misread you. Of Wes's fifteen habits, Gemma's question narrowed it to one: leaning so close to the camera that his face filled the screen, which, as the chapter on camera framing in Part IV describes, feels like someone leaning into yours. He moved the laptop back, left everything else alone, and recorded again. The next month, his conversion rate was higher than before the review began. He kept the other fourteen habits, and a client told him he seemed like a real person.

Gemma also suggested that he review one recording a month, not five a week, which he found made the reviews more useful and far less tiring.

moreCases.title: The man who recorded his partner
moreCases.scene:
Kurt, forty-one, has read this chapter and is enthusiastic about video review. He and his wife, Anna, have been arguing more than usual about
  money, and Anna has told him several times that he becomes cold and dismissive when they disagree. Kurt does not believe it. He decides to find out
  how he really comes across.

  Without telling Anna, he sets up his phone on the bookshelf to record their next conversation about the household budget. He tells himself that the
  recording is of himself, not of her, and that he will delete it after watching.

  The conversation goes badly, as usual. That night, he watches the recording. On the sound-off pass he sees what Anna had described: his arms folded,
  his eyes on his phone when she speaks, a small smile that looks like contempt when she gets upset. He is shocked. He also sees, much more clearly than
  he meant to, Anna's face as she struggles not to cry.

  Two days later, Anna finds the recording on the shared tablet, where his phone has synced it. She asks him whether he has been recording her. He says
  it was for his own practice. She says she does not care what it was for, and goes to stay with her sister for the weekend.

He also notices that he has filmed the bookshelf at an angle that shows Anna's face more clearly than his own, which he had not intended and which troubles him when he sees it.

He also realises that he cannot remember a single thing Anna said in the conversation, because he had been thinking about the recording throughout.
moreCases.misread:
Kurt read his secret recording as self-improvement, aimed at his own body. Anna read it as a breach of trust and as surveillance, which is what it was, whatever his intention.

He also read his own discovery, the folded arms and the contemptuous smile, as proof that the method worked, when the method he had used was the one this chapter forbids.

Anna had read his coldness for months as a sign that he did not care how she felt, which the recording, in its way, showed was not true: he was shocked by what he saw.
moreCases.betterRead:
This chapter is clear: everything in it is about recording your own body, and it never extends to recording other people without their knowledge. Covert recording is illegal in many places and a breach of trust everywhere, and a recording of a partner's distress during an argument is exactly the kind of material this book refuses to build files from. Kurt's discovery about his own folded arms and phone-checking was real, but it came at the cost of the very relationship he wanted to improve. The better path, which he should have taken first, was the one the chapter recommends: record himself alone, explaining something or rehearsing a difficult conversation, and ask Anna, openly, what she saw. When Anna came back, he deleted the recording in front of her, apologised without excuses and asked whether she would be willing to see a couples counsellor with him. She agreed.

Kurt also asked Anna, months later, what she saw when they argued. She told him, and he listened, and that conversation did more than the recording had.

workedReading.title: Reviewing a practice consultation
workedReading.scene:
Yusuf, thirty-nine, is a GP, and he has agreed to take part in a training session on breaking bad news. A colleague, Dr Morgan, plays a patient receiving a diagnosis of a serious illness, and the session is recorded, with both their consent, for Yusuf's own review. He will delete the file once he has made his notes. Yusuf has been told by a patient's relative, once, that he seemed "cold" when giving bad news. He does not feel cold; he feels a great deal. He wants to see what the relative saw. He sets aside forty minutes in his office after surgery, with the recording, a notebook and the three-pass method from this chapter.

He also knows that he finds these conversations harder than he lets on, and that he sometimes goes home from surgery and sits in the car for ten minutes before going in. None of that, he suspects, reaches his patients.

He also chooses to review it on the same day, before the memory of how he felt has faded, so that the felt timeline is as accurate as he can make it.

steps.label: Predict before you watch
steps.text:
Before pressing play, he writes down how he thinks he came across, and how tense he felt minute by minute, on a scale of one to ten. Harvey, Clark and colleagues found that predicting first, and then watching as if observing a stranger, made video feedback more useful for people anxious about how they come across. He writes: "Felt very tense at the start, 8; calmer once she started asking questions, 5."

He also writes down one thing he hopes he did well, so that the review is a search for gaps, not only for faults.

steps.label: First pass: get used to it
steps.text:
He watches the whole recording once, without notes. He dislikes his voice, which sounds higher and thinner than he hears it, because, as this chapter explains, he normally hears himself partly through the bones of his skull. He notices that he looks tired. He resists the urge to stop. The first viewing is for blunting the discomfort, so that the next two can be useful.

He also notices that Dr Morgan, playing the patient, is very convincing, and that the recording brings back a real consultation that went badly two years ago.

He also notices that the recording is shorter than it felt, ten minutes rather than the half hour he would have guessed.

steps.label: Second pass: sound off
steps.text:
He watches again with the sound off, noting only the body. He sees that, as he delivers the diagnosis, he looks down at his notes, his face goes completely still, and he leans back slightly in his chair. When Dr Morgan begins to cry, he looks at the computer screen. He counts four glances at the screen in the two minutes after the news. He writes each one down with its time.

He also notices that he blinks hard twice before giving the diagnosis, a small habit he has never seen, and decides it is not worth changing.

steps.label: Third pass: as a stranger
steps.text:
He watches a third time with the sound on, imagining that the doctor on the screen is a stranger. His words are kind and clear. His body, at the hardest moments, withdraws: still face, eyes down or on the screen, a lean away. He writes three neutral sentences, as the Three Passes drill suggests: "Speaks kindly. Looks away and leans back at the moments of most distress. Could seem detached."

He also notices that his words are better than he remembered, and that he had been harder on his performance than the recording justified.

He also notices that Dr Morgan, in role, looks at him several times during the silence, and that he is looking at the screen each time.

steps.label: Compare felt and seen
steps.text:
He compares his felt timeline with what he has just seen. At the moment he felt most tense, an eight, he looked calm, even flat. The tension did not show; what showed was its management, the still face and the averted eyes. Gilovich and colleagues' illusion of transparency runs in this direction: he had assumed his care was visible. It was not. What was visible was the effort of holding himself together.

He also realises that the relative who called him cold had been reading the management of his feelings, not their absence.

steps.label: Choose one habit
steps.text:
He chooses one habit to change, the one most likely to be misread: looking at the screen when a patient becomes upset. He writes a replacement, something to do rather than something to stop: turn his chair slightly towards the patient before delivering news, keep his eyes on the patient's face when they become upset, and say, "Take your time," rather than looking away. He rehearses it five times in front of the camera.

He also writes a sentence for moments when he cannot hold a patient's gaze, such as "This is hard to hear," which fills the gap with words.

He also notes the habit he will keep: his still face, which reads as calm, and which most patients find steadying.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
At the next practice session, recorded again with consent, Dr Morgan says that the consultation felt completely different, and that she felt he was with her. Yusuf compares the two recordings: no glances at the screen, a slight lean forward, his face still but turned towards her. He deletes both files after writing his notes. Months later, a patient's wife tells him, after a hard diagnosis, that he was very kind.

He also shares the method, though not the recording, with two trainees at the practice, who find their own versions of the same gap.

moreFailures.title: Reviewing only the days that went badly
moreFailures.body:
Many people reach for video review only after something has gone wrong: a bad presentation, a tense meeting, a piece of critical feedback. They record or watch that one moment and search it for flaws. The trouble is that a single recording of a bad day has no baseline. You cannot tell which of your habits are always there and which appeared under pressure, and you are likely to blame the bad outcome on whatever habit catches your eye. The chapter's pose gallery makes the point: record ordinary days too, so that the bad day has something to compare with. A recording of yourself explaining something easy, on a calm afternoon, shows you what your body does when nothing is wrong, which is exactly what you need to know before you can read what it does when something is.

A useful habit is to record one ordinary conversation for every difficult one you review.

moreFailures.title: Watching for flaws rather than gaps
moreFailures.body:
Video review often turns into a hunt for things to dislike: a double chin, a receding hairline, a nervous laugh, a voice that sounds wrong. Most of these are aesthetic, and most people who know you have long since stopped noticing them. The purpose of review, as this chapter defines it, is not to find flaws but to find gaps: places where what you feel and what others see diverge in ways that cause misreadings. Funmi's concentrating face and Yusuf's averted eyes were gaps; a dislike of one's own nose is not. Keep a separate list, if you must, of the things you simply do not like, and then leave it alone. Spend your effort on the short list of habits that change how people read you, and you will improve far faster than by trying to look better.

A simple test for any habit on your list is whether anyone has ever misread you because of it. If not, leave it.

If you notice yourself fixating on a feature you cannot change, close the recording and come back to it another day.

moreFailures.title: Comparing yourself with performers
moreFailures.body:
When people watch themselves, they often compare what they see with the speakers, actors and presenters they admire: polished, fluent, perfectly framed. Against that standard, almost everyone falls short, and the comparison can push people towards the stiff, scripted performance that Wes attempted, or towards giving up altogether. But those performers have often rehearsed for weeks, been filmed many times and had their best takes chosen for broadcast. Part IV's chapter on stage presence argues that audiences trust a body that looks as though it belongs to the person talking, not a copy of someone else's. Compare your recordings with your own earlier recordings, not with other people's best ones. The question is whether you are more readable than last month, not whether you look like a professional.

It also helps to watch the earliest recording you have of yourself alongside the latest, which usually shows more progress than you expect.

moreFailures.title: Keeping the recordings
moreFailures.body:
Recordings of yourself can feel valuable, and it is tempting to keep a library of them. But they also carry risks: they may include other people, even in the background; they may sync to shared devices, as Kurt's did; they may be seen by people you did not intend; and they may be stored on services whose terms you have not read. This chapter's advice is to delete files once the notes are written. The notes are what you need: the times, the habits, the felt and seen ratings, the one habit you chose to change. If you want to compare before and after, keep a short clip of yourself alone, stored privately, and delete it once the comparison is done. A habit of deleting is also a habit of respect for anyone who agreed to be recorded.

Check where your phone stores videos, and whether it syncs to any shared device, before you start.

And if anyone else agreed to appear, tell them when the file is gone.

questions.q: I hate watching myself. Will it get easier?
questions.a:
Yes, usually within a few viewings. Holzman and Rousey found that people reacted to recordings of their own voices with surprise and often distaste, while rating other people's recorded voices quite neutrally, and the same reaction applies to seeing yourself move. Part of the reason is that you are hearing and seeing yourself as others do, without the familiar distortions of bone-conducted sound and the reversed mirror image. Mita, Dermer and Knight found that people tend to prefer the mirror version of their own face, which is the version they see most. The first viewing in this chapter's method exists purely to blunt that discomfort. By the third or fourth recording, most people find they can watch themselves with something close to the neutral interest they would give a stranger.

It can also help to watch with the sound off first, which removes the voice that most people find hardest to bear.

It also helps to watch at normal speed, not in slow motion, since slow motion exaggerates every small movement.

A phone and something to prop it on. Set it at roughly eye level, a little further away than feels natural, so that it captures your whole upper body and your hands, and ideally your feet if you are standing. Record in a setting close to the one you want to improve: at a desk for video calls, standing for presentations, seated across a table for conversations. Use the front camera only if you can view the result unflipped, as the Mirror and Camera drill explains, because the flipped image is the mirror version, not the one others see. You do not need good lighting or sound for review; you need enough to see your body clearly. Store the files privately and delete them once you have made your notes.

It also helps to do a short test recording first, to check that your hands and face are both in frame.

questions.q: How can I record a real meeting ethically?
questions.a:
Tell everyone in advance that you will be recording your own camera feed, for your own practice, and that you will delete the file once you have made notes, as Alex did with his team. Record only your own feed, not other people's, where the platform allows it. If others will appear in the recording, ask for their agreement, and do not record anyone who declines. Never record secretly, whether at work, with friends or at home, as Kurt learned at great cost. In many places covert recording is illegal, and everywhere it breaches trust. If in doubt, record yourself alone, rehearsing the kind of conversation you want to improve, which gives you most of the benefit and none of the risk.

It also helps to tell people when you have deleted the file, which closes the loop and builds trust for next time.

questions.q: What if the recording shows something I cannot change?
questions.a:
Many things a recording shows are not habits but features: a face that looks stern at rest, a tremor, a stammer, a voice that is naturally flat, a posture shaped by injury or age. This chapter's advice is to change only what is reliably misread, and even then, sometimes the change is not to the body but to the words around it. If your resting face looks cross, you can say, as Part IV's chapter on the poker face suggests, "I'm really pleased with this, even if my face doesn't always say so." If a tremor or a condition affects how you move, a short sentence of explanation, given when you choose, can stop people misreading it. And some features are simply part of you, and the people who know you will read past them.

And remember that the people closest to you have usually adjusted to these features already, often without thinking about it.

questions.q: How often should I review recordings?
questions.a:
Not too often. For most people, one recording a month is plenty, with an extra one after you have practised a change, to see whether it has worked, as Felix and Yusuf did. More frequent review risks the opposite failure this chapter warns about: becoming absorbed in your own image and turning self-conscious in exactly the conversations you want to improve. Space between reviews also lets changes settle into habit, so that the next recording shows what you actually do rather than what you are trying to do. If you are working on something specific, such as a presentation or a hard conversation you will have to repeat, review before and after a period of practice, and then stop.

A good sign that you are reviewing too often is that you start noticing yourself during conversations rather than the other person.

questions.q: Can video review help with social anxiety?
questions.a:
It can help with some of the beliefs that feed it. Harvey, Clark and colleagues found that video feedback was more useful for people anxious about how they came across when they predicted their performance first and then watched as if observing a stranger: most found they looked far calmer than they had felt. This chapter's method builds that in. But social anxiety that affects your work, relationships or daily life is more than a habit to review on your own. If you avoid situations because of how you fear you will come across, or the anxiety causes you real distress, talk to your GP. Effective treatments exist, some of which use video feedback in a structured way with a therapist.

It can also help to review with a trusted friend, who can tell you how much of what you see others actually notice.

watch.title: Kobe Bryant: Studying Film Is About Detail
watch.notice: A basketball player on studying game film. Notice what he looks for: small details of position and timing, reviewed again and again, which is how video review of yourself works too.

reviewPrompt: Record two minutes of yourself explaining something you care about and watch it once with the sound off, as if it were a stranger. Write three neutral sentences describing that person and one guess a stranger might make about him.
